# Welcome {-}

Welcome to the learning line Quantitative Methods to Understand E&BI. Across three courses, we
will learn how to turn questions about entrepreneurship, organizations,
markets, and innovation into defensible quantitative evidence. This line will help you to learn not only how to understand research papers used in other courses and write a quantitative thesis, but also how to conduct rigorous data analysis at work.

Our aim is not simply to teach formulas or R commands. We want you to become a
careful reader and producer of evidence: someone who can choose a method,
explain its logic, interpret its output correctly, and recognize what the available data
cannot establish.

By the end of the learning line, you should be able to:

- translate an E&BI question into variables, comparisons, and testable claims;
- work reproducibly with data in R and communicate what the output means;
- conduct high-quality data analysis for work and research;
- evaluate the strength and limits of evidence in research papers; and
- design and complete a quantitative thesis.

## How to use this book

The permanent menu on the left is organized into **QM Basic**, **QM Intermediate**,
**QM Advanced**, and **Supplementary resources**. On a small (mobile) screen, open the menu
with the button at the top of the page.

Within each course, follow the chapters in order:

- **Lecture chapters** introduce you to a question and data and teach you how to conduct analysis in R and theory that allows to interpret and understand the output.
- **Tutorial chapters** help you retrieve, combine, and apply what you have
  learned. Designed for guided practice and exam preparation.
- **Course exam resources** include a cumulative formula sheet for QM Basic, a
  code-and-formula sheet for QM Intermediate, and a 100-point mock exam at the
  end of each of those courses.
- **Supplementary resources** collect reusable help with R, mathematics, and
  external videos.

IMPORTANT: Each lecture includes required pre-class preparation, in-class work, and follow-up practice. Always check and cover the material that is marked as pre-class preparation in the lecture chapter of this textbook. Be consistent with the cycle of pre-class prep, in-class joint work, after-class practice. 

## Lecture preparation and external videos

"Before class" sections include a clearly marked "Video Preparation"
box. Watch the listed required clips before the lecture and make brief notes on
the indicated concepts. Basic primarily uses MIT OpenCourseWare; Intermediate
uses Stanford's Statistical Learning series. The [External Video Guide](#videos) separates
required preparation, review when needed, and optional extension
clips. Only the first category is compulsory. In-class theory sections also
link directly to external explanations that you can replay after a lecture or an
absence. External sources may use different notation or cover more material
than this course; follow the notation and scope stated in this textbook.

## R and main dataset

You will work with R throughout all three courses. You already met R in
[Programming for E&BI](https://walshc.github.io/ebi-prog/). If a command or
workflow has become rusty, use the [R Refresher](#r-refresher) and the earlier
course as references.

Our shared dataset records pitches shown on the US television programme
*Shark Tank*. In a televised pitch, entrepreneurs present a venture or product
to a panel of investors known as sharks. They may ask for money in exchange
for an ownership share; the investors question them, negotiate, and may
announce an agreement during the episode.

Most chapters use a 19-variable teaching view derived from the
[Shark Tank US Dataset](https://www.kaggle.com/datasets/thirumani/shark-tank-us-dataset).
One row represents one recorded televised pitch. The file contains 1,441
pitches from completed Seasons 1--16; incomplete Season 17 is excluded. Its
variables include pitch and episode identifiers, venture industry and written
description, the initial amount and equity requested, whether an agreement was
announced on air, recorded deal terms, and the source's broad
presenter-gender-composition category.

This is an observational record of selected, edited television pitches—not a
random sample of all entrepreneurs or ventures. An on-air agreement is not
evidence that the investment was completed or that the venture later
succeeded. The data can describe recorded pitches and associations among their
variables, but they do not by themselves identify causal effects.

## Tutorials and assessment

All three courses end with an exam with open-ended questions that account for 100% of the grade.
In QM Basic, the written exam can ask you to verify, interpret, and describe
supplied R output and solve probability and statistics tasks. In QM
Intermediate and QM Advanced, you will work directly with data in R during an
exam administered through TestVision. Tutorials in all courses are designed as
exam preparation sessions.

Go directly to the [QM Basic Formula Sheet](#formula-sheet), [QM Basic Mock
Exam](#basic-mock-exam), [QM Intermediate Code
Sheet](#intermediate-code-sheet), or [QM Intermediate Mock
Exam](#intermediate-mock-exam) when preparing for assessment.

## Working with  AI

We provide a chatbot for this course: [Tilly for QM Courseline](https://chatbot.tilburg.ai/). It is designed to support and guide you throughout the course. It can help with organizational questions (schedule, grade composition, etc) as well as act as an individual tutor when solving tasks together. You can also ask it to generate additional practice questions to prepare for the exam.

When you use AI, follow **Attempt → Ask → Verify → Explain**:

1. Attempt to solve the question yourself and identify where you are stuck.
2. Ask AI for support in the form of a hint, counterexample, or diagnostic question. Be precise and detailed when creating a prompt for AI (better prompt - better answer).
3. Verify the response against the data, course notation, and R output. Verification becomes the key skill when working with AI.
4. Explain the result in your own words to internalize the knowledge. Ask AI for feedback on this explanation and/or bring it as a question to lectures/tutorials and your classmates.
